title: Redactame
tagline: A voice-first Android keyboard that turns how you talk into how you meant to write it.
summary: An Android input method (IME) built around voice and AI: speak casually, and it transcribes and reformulates the text into something appropriate to send — including across languages.

caseStudy.context: Typing on a phone is slow, and the register we speak in is rarely the register we want to send. Redactame starts from voice instead of the keyboard.
caseStudy.problem: How do you go from informal, spoken thoughts to a clean, appropriately-worded message — sometimes in another language — without losing meaning or inventing things that weren't said?
caseStudy.idea: A keyboard (IME) you talk to. It listens, transcribes, and rewrites: fixing register, tightening phrasing, and optionally translating — Spanish → French / English being the primary path.
caseStudy.solution: The current focus is the voice → transcription → reformulation → send loop, with a hard rule that reformulation must preserve meaning and never fabricate information the speaker didn't provide.
goals: Speak informally and get send-ready text back.
Reformulate for appropriateness while preserving intent.
Support transformation between languages, especially Spanish → French / English.
Preserve meaning — never invent facts that weren't said.
Research local / on-device processing and privacy tradeoffs.
decisions: __EDITABLE__ Technical decisions will be documented here as they are made. Nothing below is claimed as implemented yet.
caseStudy.architecture: __EDITABLE__ Architecture notes to be added as the IME, speech and reformulation layers take shape.
challenges: __EDITABLE__ Latency of the voice → text → rewrite loop on a phone.
__EDITABLE__ Keeping reformulation faithful to the original meaning.
__EDITABLE__ On-device vs. remote processing and what that means for privacy.

title: Personal Atlas
tagline: This site — a spatial, photography-first way to explore a person instead of a résumé.
summary: A personal portfolio built as a spatial card navigator: the home page is the browser, each section is a card, and the whole atmosphere reacts to what you've selected.

caseStudy.context: Most developer portfolios read like a template — hero, logos, three project cards, contact. This one treats a life as an atlas of overlapping interests.
caseStudy.problem: How do you present software, AI, photography, skating, languages, music and places as one coherent, explorable space rather than a list?
caseStudy.idea: Make the home page a spatial carousel. A dominant central card, receding side cards, and a background that re-colours the entire page to match the active section — the way selecting a trip re-grades the whole scene.
caseStudy.solution: A data-driven system: one carousel and one card component render every section from a single JSON source. A reactive background crossfades atmospheres, and clicking the active card expands it into the section via shared-layout transitions.
goals: Home page that works as the portfolio's navigator.
Reactive, cinematic background tied to the active section.
Content fully data-driven and editable without touching components.
First-class desktop and mobile behaviour, with reduced-motion support.
decisions: Single source of truth for content in a shared `content/` directory read by both the SPA and the API.
Framer Motion for physical carousel motion and shared-layout card → page transitions.
CSS-transform-only animation (no WebGL) for performance and accessibility.
FastAPI backend for the GitHub integration and contact form so no secrets touch the browser.
caseStudy.architecture: Vite + React SPA with React Router; FastAPI service exposing sections, projects, curated GitHub repos and a validated contact endpoint backed by SQLite.
challenges: Keeping the carousel motion physical rather than index-swapping.
Crossfading full-screen atmospheres without flashes or layout shift.
Making the spatial layout degrade gracefully to a single-card mobile view.
learnings: A strict data-driven contract makes a 10-section site trivial to reorder and grow.
Shared-layout transitions carry most of the 'cinematic' feeling at almost no runtime cost.
